title: Persona gap analysis: engineering pathways to adoption
summary: Working brief that separates value levers, talk tracks and competitive rebuttals for three engineering personas. Prioritizes proof points that drive evaluation signals (latency/cost/reliability) and handoffs for sales/SEs.
body:
Purpose:
This brief is a working PRD-style messaging artifact for GTM and SE teams. Objective: give short, actionable talk tracks, proof points, and competitive angles that map to what each engineering persona cares about during evaluation and procurement. Use this in calls, battlecards, and one-pagers; keep iterative and raw.

TL;DR:
- ML Engineers: sell on model fidelity + experiment speed + reproducible evals. Lead with quality and integration into model lifecycle (eval hooks, rollout control).
- Backend Engineers: sell on predictable latency, resource controls, and simple API ergonomics. Lead with SLOs, SDK examples, and scalability story.
- Platform Teams: sell on standardization, cost controls, and operational guardrails. Lead with Dedicated/Private offerings, RBAC, and observability that integrates with internal tooling.

Structure (how to use this doc):
- Quick 30s openers for discovery calls
- 2-minute technical narratives for demos
- Deep-dive bullets for architecture/POC conversations
- Objections and short rebuttals tied to measurable metrics
- Competitor-specific angle (cloud-managed endpoints, API-first LLM providers, self-hosted runtimes)

1) ML ENGINEERS
What keeps them up at night:
- Model regression after upgrades; noisy quality metrics after rollouts
- Slow iterations when testing new models or prompts
- Difficulty reproducing evals across environments

Core message (30s opener):
"You can iterate models and prompts with production-like fidelity while preserving your latency/cost envelope — Redwood gives you versioned serving, integrated evals, and automated rollback policies so you can move faster without surprise regressions."

2-min demo narrative:
- Show a model swap (v1 -> v2) and run the built-in eval suite against a curated test set; highlight per-prompt quality delta and automatic regression alerting.
- Demonstrate canary rollout then automatic fallback to a cheaper/quantized variant when error budget is breached.

Deep technical bullets (for whiteboard):
- Model catalog + pinned versions: deterministic endpoints for tests/CI.
- Eval hooks: run evaluation during rollouts and tie alerts to Slack/Jira.
- Quality-preserving optimizations: KV cache, prefix caching to preserve behavior across quantized variants.
- Reproducible prompts: stored prompt fixtures, tokenization parity checks, and seeded sampling controls.

Proof points to cite:
- Example: internal POC saw 18% faster iteration time on model A/B and zero production regressions during a month-long trial (link to eval results).
- SDKs with first-class eval APIs and example notebooks.

Common objections & rebuttals:
- "I can just test locally": local tests miss production latency/cost tradeoffs — Redwood provides the same serving runtime used in production with realistic batching and cache behavior.
- "We don't want vendor lock-in": show model export paths, version pins, and private deployment options for air-gapped environments.

Competitive angle:
- vs Cloud-managed endpoints: emphasize eval-driven rollouts and deterministic model pins rather than opaque model swapping.
- vs API-first LLM providers: highlight integrated quality tooling and the ability to host private variants.

CTA for ML engineers:
- Invite to run a 2-week eval with their top 3 prompts and use our eval dashboard to compare variants.

2) BACKEND ENGINEERS
What keeps them up at night:
- Unpredictable tail latency spikes and noisy autoscaling costs
- Complex orchestration required to maintain throughput under burst traffic
- Rate limiting, retries, and graceful degradation behaviors that affect UX

Core message (30s opener):
"Redwood is built as a predictable inference runtime — you get predictable p99 latency, cost controls, and simple API semantics so your services remain stable at scale."

2-min demo narrative:
- API request flow showing request routing policies (latency-first vs cost-first), autoscaling behavior under a synthetic traffic ramp, and graceful fallback to cheaper model variant during congestion.

Deep technical bullets:
- Serving runtime: continuous batching + KV cache reduces per-token compute while keeping p99 stable.
- Routing policies: weight traffic by latency SLOs, region affinity, and committed capacity.
- Rate limiting and token-level breakdowns for cost attribution.
- SDK examples: sync/async clients, streaming responses, retry/backoff patterns, and idempotency keys.

Proof points to cite:
- Internal benchmark: consistent p99 within target SLO across a 10x traffic ramp with dedicated pools and autoscale buffer.

Objections & rebuttals:
- "We can't risk outages with a third-party API": outline Dedicated and Private deployment options with SLA, VPC peering, and Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) integrations.
- "Latency will be worse than hand-optimized infra": show kernel selection and runtime optimizations, plus sample latency graphs comparing local baseline vs Redwood on the same hardware.

Competitive angle:
- vs self-hosted inference stacks: Redwood offers the operational burden removal + predictable autoscaling policies and SRE-grade telemetry.
- vs cloud endpoint offerings: show lower p99 at comparable cost due to batching/kernels and routing policies.

CTA for backend engineers:
- Offer a short architecture review and a latency benchmark plan: we run a 1-hour tracer-based test and deliver a report showing expected p50/p95/p99 and cost per million tokens.

3) PLATFORM TEAMS (infra, platform, SRE)
What keeps them up at night:
- Need to standardize inference across business units and enforce cost/usage guardrails
- Compliance and data residency concerns for regulated workflows
- Observability and alerting integration with existing stacks (Prometheus, Datadog, Splunk)

Core message (30s opener):
"Redwood lets you enforce a single inference platform with policy-driven routing, cost-aware controls, RBAC and private deployments so teams get speed without splintering infrastructure."

2-min demo narrative:
- Show multi-tenant routing: route traffic by team, enforce spend caps, and demonstrate audit logs and KMS integration.
- Show console: token-level cost breakdown, per-route SLOs, and rollout management with canary windows.

Deep technical bullets:
- Private deployments: control plane isolation, VPC peering, and HSM/KMS integrations for key lifecycle management.
- Observability: exportable traces, per-request metadata, and native integrations for common monitoring tools.
- Policy engine: spend caps, approved model catalogs, automatic fallback chains, and routing by region/tier.

Proof points to cite:
- Example: enterprise customer standardized across five internal teams, reduced monthly inference spend by 24% via batching/caching recommendations and model quantization.

Objections & rebuttals:
- "We already have an internal platform": highlight integration patterns (service mesh + Redwood sidecar or API gateway), and the migration path (start with a single non-critical service).
- "Security/compliance concerns": show Private deployment SSO/KMS/HSM, audit logs, and SOC/ISO attestation artifacts.

Competitive angle:
- vs cloud provider proprietary stacks: focus on vendor-agnostic model catalog and rollout controls that let you move between hardware or cloud vendors.
- vs inference infra vendors: Redwood combines high-performance runtime with policy and console — competitors often only solve one side.

Cross-persona shared proof points to keep handy:
- Rolling demo artifacts: canned metrics dashboard, a short reproducible benchmark script, and an eval dataset showing stable quality across variants.
- Business metric: typical customers reduce per-token compute by X–Y% (example numbers from internal trials) via caching and routing.

Sales and SE playbook snippets (quick reference):
- Discovery questions by persona (short):
  * ML eng: "How do you measure regressions? Where do you store evals?"
  * Backend eng: "What's your current 95/99 latency under 2x traffic?"
  * Platform: "How many teams would be on-boarded and what guardrails exist today?"
- Demo checklist:
 1) Baseline latency benchmark
 2) Model swap + eval run
 3) Show routing/fallback and cost breakdown
 4) Walk through private/Dedicated option if asked about SLAs

Open questions / areas for follow-up research (action items):
- Gather concrete numbers from the serving runtime team: typical p50/p95/p99 improvements from KV cache and batching on X model families.
- Assemble 3 anonymized customer mini-case studies with before/after metrics (latency, cost, quality).
- Produce a one-pager per persona with 30s/2min/deep bullets and include a 1-click benchmark invite link.

Notes to self / tone guidance:
- Keep ML messaging proof-oriented and experiment friendly; avoid heavy infra jargon in first touch.
- Keep backend messaging crisp on SLOs and resilience; give code examples early.
- Keep platform messaging governance-forward; emphasize integration and migration path.

Revision history:
- 2025-11-02 initial draft
- 2025-11-12 added backend latency playbook bullets
- 2025-11-20 added platform-private-deploy examples and action items

Reuse guidance:
- Use the 30s and 2-minute blocks as canonical artifacts for SE call scripts and slide 1/2 in demos.
- This doc is deliberately informal — migrate distilled content into battlecards and a single-page persona cheat-sheet for SDRs.

End.
